blocks.text: Stereoisomers are of two types: optical isomers and cis-trans isomers (next topic). Optical isomers have identical physical and chemical properties except their ability to rotate plane-polarised light. Such isomers are optically active, and the rotation of the plane of polarisation is optical activity. If a compound rotates the plane to the right (clockwise) it is dextrorotatory, shown (+); if to the left (anticlockwise), laevorotatory, shown (-).

blocks.title: Keep in mind: the polarimeter
blocks.text: A polarimeter detects and measures optical activity. Monochromatic light (one wavelength) is passed through a polariser so that it vibrates in one plane, then through a solution of the compound. If the plane is rotated, the compound is optically active; if not, it is optically inactive.

blocks.alt: Unpolarised light (a circle with arrows in all directions) passes through a polarizer (a circle with a narrow vertical slit) to give PPL (a circle with one vertical double arrow), then through a box labelled Sample. Two arrows leave the sample: to a circle where a dashed double arrow is turned clockwise from the vertical, with a clockwise curved arrow (Dextrorotatory), and to a circle where it is turned anticlockwise, with an anticlockwise curved arrow (Levorotatory).
blocks.caption: Figure 19.4: Optical rotation of PPL (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.4).

blocks.text: The basic requirement for optical activity is that the molecule is non-superimposable on its mirror image. Our left and right hands are the everyday example: they are mirror images, but one cannot be placed exactly on the other. Molecules that can be superimposed on their mirror images are achiral and optically inactive.

blocks.alt: A left hand (palm towards the viewer, thumb on the right), a mirror, and a right hand (thumb on the left) as its mirror image; then the two hands laid one on the other, labelled nonsuperimposable, with the thumbs pointing opposite ways.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.5: Our hands are non-superimposable on their mirror images (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.5).

blocks.title: Chiral carbon
blocks.text: A chiral (asymmetric) carbon is a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups. A molecule with only one chiral carbon is always chiral and optically active; a molecule with more than one may or may not be.

Lactic acid, CH3-CH(OH)-COOH, has one chiral carbon bonded to CH3, H, OH and COOH. In three dimensions it exists as two stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images: enantiomers (from the Greek enantio, opposite). Enantiomers have identical physical and chemical properties but rotate plane-polarised light by the same amount in opposite directions, and they can act differently in living systems. A 50:50 mixture of the (+) and (-) forms is optically inactive; it is a racemic mixture, written with (+/-) before the name. So lactic acid exists as (+)-lactic acid, (-)-lactic acid and the inactive racemic mixture.

blocks.alt: Left: CH3-C*H(OH)-COOH with the carbons numbered 3, 2, 1 and an asterisk on carbon 2 (OH above, H below). Middle: (-) lactic acid, the starred C with CH3 up, HOOC down-left, H on a hashed bond to the right and OH on a solid wedge down-right. A dashed vertical mirror line. Right: (+) lactic acid, its mirror image: CH3 up, COOH down-right, H hashed to the left and HO on a wedge down-left.
blocks.caption: Lactic acid and its two enantiomers, (-) and (+) lactic acid (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: Stereoisomers that contain at least two similar chiral carbons and also have a plane of symmetry are optically inactive. The plane divides the molecule into two halves that are mirror images of each other; each half would rotate the plane of polarised light in the opposite direction, so the rotations cancel inside the molecule (internal compensation). Such stereoisomers are meso forms; meso-tartaric acid is the classic example.

blocks.alt: A yellow box. Two Fischer projections of tartaric acid either side of a dashed vertical line labelled 'Mirror': left COOH, H-C-OH, H-C-OH, COOH; right COOH, HO-C-H, HO-C-H, COOH. A dashed horizontal line through the middle of both is labelled 'Plane of symmetry'. Below: '1 and 2 are Identical and represent meso form of tartaric acid'.
blocks.caption: Meso form of tartaric acid (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.title: How many optical isomers?
blocks.text: The maximum number of optical isomers is 2^n, where n is the number of chiral carbon atoms. The number is smaller if two or more chiral carbons are similar.
